    4|       |//! Argon2 (RFC 9106) as implemented by BouncyCastle's `Argon2BytesGenerator`, the engine
    5|       |//! behind WarpLib's `ARGON2`.
    6|       |//!
    7|       |//! The port follows the Java class line by line: same parameter validation (and error texts),
    8|       |//! same memory alignment (`memory` rounded down to a multiple of `4 * lanes` blocks, at least

   11|       |//! lengths that are only known at run time.

    4|       |//! Student's t distribution of Commons Math (`TDistribution`): its cumulative probability
    5|       |//! (`Beta.regularizedBeta`) and its inverse (`AbstractRealDistribution`'s bracketing then
    6|       |//! `BrentSolver`), as the outlier tests of Warp 10 use them.
    7|       |//!
    8|       |//! Only what `TDistribution` needs is ported: the regularized beta function is evaluated with
    9|       |//! `b = 1/2` (or `a = 1/2` after its symmetry), so `logBeta` reduces to its branch for a
   10|       |//! smallest argument below 1, and `Gamma.gamma` to arguments in `(0, 20]`. Commons Math
   11|       |//! computes with `FastMath`, the port with the standard library: results may differ in the
   12|       |//! last bits.
   13|       |
   14|       |#![allow(clippy::many_single_char_names)] // the names of Commons Math
   15|       |
   16|       |use crate::error::Result;
   17|       |use crate::error::math::MathError;
   18|       |

    3|       |//! Finite numbers at the edges.
    4|       |//!
    5|       |//! Inside the WarpScript evaluator `NaN` and the infinities are ordinary `DOUBLE` values, as in
    6|       |//! Warp 10 (the `NaN` literal, the `NaN NaN` of a datapoint without location, `1.0 0.0 /`).
    7|       |//! A number that enters from outside the evaluator (HTTP, a command line, a datastore) or that
    8|       |//! leaves it for a format which cannot represent those values is checked with
    9|       |//! [`ensure_finite`]: a non-finite number is a typed failure there, never a value to store,

   23|       |    NegativeInfinity,
   24|       |}

    4|       |//! Collection functions of WarpLib: conversions between the stack and lists, sets and maps
    5|       |//! (`LIST->`, `UNLIST`, `MAP->`…), set algebra, element access and mutation (`GET`, `SET`,
    6|       |//! `PUT`, `REMOVE`, `SUBLIST`, `SUBMAP`…), structural helpers (`FLATTEN`, `ZIP`, `CLONE`,
    7|       |//! `REVERSE`, `UNIQUE`, `SIZE`), `MAPID` and the bulk variable stores (`LSTORE`, `MSTORE` and
    8|       |//! their conditional variants).
    9|       |//!
   10|       |//! The macro-driven functions (`LMAP`, `LFILTER`, `SORTBY`…) and the sorts live in
   11|       |//! [`super::functional`], `PACK` / `UNPACK` in [`super::pack`].
   12|       |//!
   13|       |//! # Reference semantics
   14|       |//!
   15|       |//! Lists, maps and sets are shared handles: the functions that mutate their operand in Java
   16|       |//! (`SET`, `PUT`, `REMOVE`, `REVERSE`, `APPEND`…) mutate the shared object here too, while the
   17|       |//! ones that build a new collection (`CLONEREVERSE`, `SUBLIST`, `UNIQUE`…) leave the operand
   18|       |//! untouched. Byte arrays are immutable in this runtime, so `SET` and `REVERSE` on `BYTES`
   19|       |//! push a modified copy instead of altering the operand in place.
   20|       |//!
   21|       |//! # Operands that are not modelled
   22|       |//!
   23|       |//! Geo Time Series, encoders, matrices and vectors are not modelled yet (`->V` builds a plain
   24|       |//! list); the functions that accept them in Java raise the error a script gets for an
   25|       |//! unsupported type. Strings are indexed by UTF-16 code unit like in Java. See
   26|       |//! `docs/DIVERGENCES.md`.

    4|       |//! Filling the gaps of Geo Time Series: `FILL` (driving the fillers of [`crate::fillers`]),
    5|       |//! `FILLVALUE`, `FILLPREVIOUS`, `FILLNEXT`, `FILLTICKS` and `INTERPOLATE` — the `fill*`
    6|       |//! methods of `GTSHelper` and `INTERPOLATE.interpolate`.
    7|       |//!
    8|       |//! Like Warp 10, the fills read the series they fill live: a macro filler, which adds its
    9|       |//! datapoints to the original series rather than to the filled copy, makes the bucket and
   10|       |//! cross fills run until a limit of the stack stops them.

  201|       |/// `GTSHelper.crossProduct` of the datapoints `a`, `b` and `c` (tick, value).
  202|    217|fn cross_product(gts: &GeoTimeSerie, a: usize, b: usize, c: usize) -> f64 {
  203|    217|    let (ax, ay) = (gts.ticks[a] as f64, double(&gts.value_at(a)));
  204|    217|    let (bx, by) = (gts.ticks[b] as f64, double(&gts.value_at(b)));
  205|    217|    let (cx, cy) = (gts.ticks[c] as f64, double(&gts.value_at(c)));
  206|    217|    (ax - bx) * (cy - by) - (ay - by) * (cx - bx)
  207|    217|}

   11|       |//! custom serializers of `io.warp10.json` are honoured: `BYTES` become the ISO-8859-1 string of
   12|       |//! the bytes, macros and named functions their `toString()`, and the objects Jackson cannot
   13|       |//! serialise as beans (`BITSET`, `MARK`, contexts, `MATCHER`…) become `null`.
   14|       |//!
   15|       |//! Parsing follows Jackson's strict mapper configuration: non-numeric numbers (`NaN`,
   16|       |//! `Infinity`, `-INF`…) and missing array values (`[1,,2]`) are accepted, trailing tokens are
   17|       |//! rejected, integers become `LONG`s and other numbers `DOUBLE`s.
   18|       |//!
   19|       |//! Not ported yet (`io.warp10.json`): the serializers of Geo Time Series, GTS encoders,
   20|       |//! `Metadata`, `RealVector` / `RealMatrix` and audit statements — none of those types exist in
   21|       |//! the runtime so far.
   22|       |

  422|       |/// Parse `input` like `JsonUtils.jsonToObject` followed by `JSONTO.transform`: objects become

    4|       |//! Bit packing functions of WarpLib: `PACK` and `UNPACK`.
    5|       |//!
    6|       |//! A format string describes a sequence of fields: `<` (little endian) or `>` (big endian)
    7|       |//! followed by `L` or `U` and a decimal bit length (signed or unsigned integer, 64 bits when
    8|       |//! the length is omitted) or by `D` (a 64-bit double); `B` (one bit, `false` / `true`); `S` or
    9|       |//! `s` and a length (skipped bits, written as ones or zeros by `PACK`). Bits are packed most
   10|       |//! significant first; `PACK` pads the last byte with zeros and `UNPACK` reads zeros past the
   11|       |//! end of the data.
   12|       |//!
   13|       |//! The format is scanned by UTF-16 code unit like in Java, and lengths are accumulated with
   14|       |//! Java `int` arithmetic (`L4294967297` is `L1`).
   15|       |

    4|       |//! A model of the iteration order of `java.util.HashMap` (and `HashSet`).
    5|       |//!
    6|       |//! Some Warp 10 results are Java hash maps whose iteration order leaks into WarpScript (the
    7|       |//! maps a pickle decodes to, the maps a pickle is written from). [`JavaHashMap`] reproduces
    8|       |//! that order: buckets indexed by the spread hash code, insertion order within a bucket,
    9|       |//! the table doubling when the size exceeds three quarters of the capacity. Bins are never
   10|       |//! turned into trees (Java does so past 8 colliding keys in a table of 64 buckets or more).
   11|       |

    4|       |//! The Thrift structures `GTSWrapper` and `Metadata` that `WRAP` / `UNWRAP` serialize, with
    5|       |//! the compact protocol of libthrift 0.17 (`TCompactProtocol` over a `TMemoryInputTransport`)
    6|       |//! that Warp 10 uses through `TSerializer` / `TDeserializer`.
    7|       |//!
    8|       |//! Decoding reproduces the reader faithfully, malformed input included: the unchecked "fast"
    9|       |//! varint path that runs off the end of the array, the missing negative length check of
   10|       |//! binary fields, the `MaxMessageSize` accounting of containers, the skipping of unknown
   11|       |//! fields and of fields of an unexpected type. A [`ThriftError`] is either a malformed payload
   12|       |//! (what `TDeserializer` reports as a `TException`, which callers wrap as the cause of their own
   13|       |//! message) or a defect of the reader that escapes unwrapped (see
   14|       |//! [`ThriftError::is_malformed_input`]).

    4|       |//! The dynamic value type held on the WarpScript stack.
    5|       |//!
    6|       |//! Warp 10 stacks hold arbitrary Java objects; [`Value`] is the closed set of types the Rust
    7|       |//! runtime knows. Containers (`LIST`, `MAP`, `SET`, GTS…) have **reference semantics** exactly
    8|       |//! like in Java: `DUP` yields another handle to the same list, `CLONE` deep-copies.
    9|       |//!
   10|       |//! Equality and hashing follow Java's `equals` / `hashCode` contracts (a `LONG` never equals a
   11|       |//! `DOUBLE`, `NaN` equals `NaN` as a map key…). The numeric comparison used by `==`, `<`… is a
   12|       |//! separate function in the function library.
   13|       |
